answers.text: Give it this: from the supplier email, always return exactly three lines in this order - delivery date, item and quantity, then any change from the original order. That way you get the same three lines every time, whichever email it's reading.

Instruction: list every expense line with date, amount, category and submitter, then add a total for the week worked out by adding the amount column. If two lines look like the same claim entered twice, list both but flag the second one for a check rather than dropping it.

The line about the revised delivery date doesn't add up. The call was on the 14th and it says the new date is the 19th, 'three days out' - that's five days, not three. I'd flag this before the email goes out.

The on-time rate looks off - 3 late out of 62 deliveries works out closer to 95%, not the 97% written here. Also, stock is said to be steady at 340 units even though deliveries went up 15% that week, and nothing explains why that wouldn't move the count. I'd get both checked before this goes up.

I'd sign off the second one - it shows the actual sales and returns figures so anyone can redo the maths and get 4.1%. The first one might well be correct too, but there's no way to check it without rerunning the numbers yourself.
I'd send the second reply, it has the order reference and the credit reference so it can be looked up. The first one just says sorry and gives a credit without saying which order or how much.
1. No, I'd leave that out. 2. Yes, that's fine. 3. No, I'd leave that one out too. 4. Yes, go ahead with that one. 5. No, wouldn't put that in either.
I'd take out the pricing and discount figures before pasting anything in, and I'd be careful with the confidentiality clause too since it names both companies directly. Not sure what else I'd change.
I usually just check the totals against the source sheet before it goes out to my manager - seems like enough to catch the obvious problems.

The step I'd put a gate on is the automatic send at the end, step 4 - once it's gone out, it's gone out. I'd have it flag anything where the extracted quantities look unusually high or where stock is right on the cutoff, rather than letting it send straight away. The extraction step at the start matters too, since a wrong read carries through the rest.
